module_intro.note: 1.1 Introduction: motivational text and a tally-stick photo; previews the chapter (real numbers, surds, rounding, factorisation). No teaching items.

lesson.notes: The exercise mixes objectives within single questions (Q7 spans objective-1 and objective-2). Each exercise is mapped to its main objective; verifiers may split parts.

items.quote: A rational number (Q) is any number which can be written as
items.claim: A rational number is any number a/b with a and b integers and b ≠ 0.

provenance.by: Claude, from the PDF text layer and page images, 2026-10-07

items.quote: all integers are rational numbers
items.claim: All integers are rational, because they can be written with denominator 1.

items.quote: Irrational numbers (Q′) are numbers that cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Irrational numbers cannot be written as a fraction with integer numerator and denominator.

items.claim: A fraction with denominator zero is undefined.

items.quote: not all decimal numbers are rational numbers
items.claim: Every rational number can be written as a decimal, but not every decimal is rational. Rational decimals terminate (4/10 = 0,4), repeat one digit (1/3 = 0,3̇), or repeat a block (2/11 = 0,(18) with a bar).

items.quote: You can use a dot or a bar over the repeated digits
items.claim: A dot or a bar over repeated digits marks a recurring decimal; a bar over several digits means all of them recur. Dot and bar are equivalent: 0,3̇ = 0,3̄ = 0,333...

provenance.by: Claude, from the PDF text layer and page images, 2026-10-07

items.quote: first write the number in decimal form
items.claim: To decide rational or irrational: write it as a decimal. Terminating means rational; otherwise look for a repeated pattern; no repeated pattern means irrational.

items.claim: Rounding an irrational number gives a rational approximation of it.
